series.title: Germany 1914–1989
series.subtitle: The story before you go
series.intro: The big picture in five chapters, from the Kaiser's empire to the fall of the Wall. Start here.

chapters.title: Empire and the Great War
chapters.text:
To understand twentieth-century Germany, we have to start a little earlier, in 1871. In that year, after a short and victorious war against France, the many German states were united into a single empire, proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. Its emperor, the Kaiser, was the King of Prussia, and its capital was Berlin. The architect of unification was the Prussian chancellor, Otto von Bismarck.

The new Germany grew at astonishing speed. Within a generation it became an industrial giant, with coal and steel in the Ruhr, a world-leading chemical and electrical industry, and the best universities in Europe. Berlin's population exploded, from under a million to around two million people, with grand boulevards, department stores, and crowded tenement blocks for the workers. Germany had a parliament, the Reichstag, elected by all adult men, and the largest socialist party in Europe. But real power rested with the Kaiser, his ministers and the army, and the officer corps, dominated by Prussian aristocrats, enjoyed enormous prestige.

In 1888, the young Wilhelm the Second became Kaiser. He dismissed Bismarck and pursued a more aggressive policy, demanding for Germany a place in the sun: colonies, and a navy to rival Britain's. Europe divided into two armed camps. Germany and Austria-Hungary on one side; France, Russia and, increasingly, Britain on the other.

In June 1914, the heir to the Austrian throne was assassinated in Sarajevo. Germany gave Austria-Hungary unconditional support, the so-called blank cheque, and within weeks a regional crisis became a continental war. Germany's war plan, drawn up by General von Schlieffen, called for a rapid knockout blow against France through neutral Belgium, before turning east against Russia. The invasion of Belgium brought Britain into the war.

In August 1914, crowds in Berlin cheered the troops, and many believed the war would be over by Christmas. Instead, the German advance was stopped at the river Marne, near Paris, and the Western Front froze into a line of trenches from the Channel to Switzerland. For four years, millions of men fought over a few kilometres of mud, at places like Verdun and the Somme. In the east, the war was more mobile, and Germany won great victories over Russia.

At home, the British naval blockade caused severe shortages. The winter of 1916 to 1917 became known as the turnip winter, when hundreds of thousands of civilians died of hunger and disease. The army's supreme command, under Generals Hindenburg and Ludendorff, effectively ran the country. In 1917, the United States entered the war, and Russia collapsed into revolution. Germany imposed a harsh peace on the new Bolshevik regime and, in the spring of 1918, threw everything into a final offensive in the west. It failed.

By the autumn of 1918, the German army was exhausted and retreating, and its allies were falling away. Ludendorff himself demanded an armistice, but he made sure that civilian politicians would be the ones to ask for it. At the beginning of November, sailors at Kiel mutinied rather than sail out for a last suicidal battle. The revolt spread across the country. On the ninth of November, in Berlin, the Kaiser's abdication was announced, and a republic was proclaimed from the Reichstag. Wilhelm fled to exile in the Netherlands. Two days later, on the eleventh of November, the armistice was signed.

About two million German soldiers had died. And because the war ended while German troops still stood on foreign soil, many Germans refused to believe they had really been defeated. Instead, a poisonous legend spread: that the army had been stabbed in the back by socialists, Jews and politicians at home. This lie would haunt the new republic from its very first day.

chapters.title: The Weimar Republic
chapters.text:
The republic born in November 1918 took its name from the small town of Weimar, where its constitution was written, far from the violence of Berlin. On paper it was one of the most democratic states in the world. Women could vote for the first time, and a system of proportional representation gave a voice to every political current. But the republic faced enemies on both sides from the very start.

In January 1919, communists tried to seize power in Berlin. The Social Democratic government turned to the army and to the Freikorps, volunteer units of former soldiers, to crush the uprising. The communist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht were captured and murdered. The left never forgave the Social Democrats. Meanwhile, the right never forgave the republic for accepting defeat.

In June 1919, Germany signed the Treaty of Versailles. It lost territory, including Alsace-Lorraine and land to the new Polish state, all its colonies, and most of its army. It accepted responsibility for the war and was required to pay reparations. Almost every German, from left to right, considered the treaty a humiliation. Nationalists called the politicians who had signed it the November criminals. In 1920, right-wing soldiers attempted a coup in Berlin, the Kapp Putsch, which collapsed after a general strike. Political murders became common: the foreign minister, Walther Rathenau, a Jew, was shot dead in 1922.

Then came 1923, the year of chaos. When Germany fell behind on reparations, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, the industrial heart of the country. The government responded by printing money, and inflation spiralled out of control. By November, a loaf of bread cost two hundred billion marks. People carried wages in wheelbarrows, and the savings of the middle class were wiped out. In Munich, an obscure agitator named Adolf Hitler tried to launch a national revolution from a beer hall. The putsch failed, Hitler went to prison, and there he wrote Mein Kampf.

And then, surprisingly, things got better. A new currency stopped the inflation. American loans flowed in, and reparations were rescheduled. Under foreign minister Gustav Stresemann, Germany made peace with France and joined the League of Nations. These were the Golden Twenties. Berlin became the most exciting city in Europe: the city of cabaret and jazz, of the Bauhaus and expressionist cinema, of Bertolt Brecht, Marlene Dietrich and Albert Einstein. It was also a city of open homosexual life and of sharp social contrasts.

The stability was fragile. In October 1929, Stresemann died, and weeks later the Wall Street crash ended the flow of American money. Germany was hit harder than almost any other country. By 1932, six million Germans were unemployed. The parliamentary system broke down: parties could not agree on a majority, and from 1930 chancellors governed by emergency decree, signed by the president, the old war hero Paul von Hindenburg.

The crisis was Hitler's opportunity. His National Socialist German Workers' Party, the Nazis, promised work, national rebirth, and revenge on the enemies supposedly responsible for Germany's misery: the Versailles powers, the Marxists, and above all, the Jews. Its brown-shirted stormtroopers, the SA, fought communists in the streets. In 1928 the Nazis won less than three percent of the vote. In July 1932, they won thirty-seven percent and became the largest party in the Reichstag. The communists also grew. The democratic centre was collapsing.

Hitler never won a majority in a free election. He came to power through a deal. A small group of conservative politicians around Hindenburg, led by the former chancellor Franz von Papen, believed they could use Hitler's mass movement and keep him under control. On the thirtieth of January 1933, Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor of Germany, in a cabinet where Nazis were a minority. That night, the SA marched with torches through the Brandenburg Gate. Papen boasted that within two months they would have pushed Hitler into a corner. He could not have been more wrong.

chapters.title: The Nazi Dictatorship
chapters.text:
It took Hitler barely eighteen months to destroy German democracy. On the twenty-seventh of February 1933, the Reichstag building burned. A young Dutch communist was arrested at the scene, and the Nazis claimed it was the signal for a communist uprising. The next day, Hindenburg signed an emergency decree suspending freedom of speech, of the press and of assembly. Thousands of communists and social democrats were arrested, beaten and held in improvised camps, often in cellars run by the SA. One of the first permanent concentration camps opened at Dachau, near Munich, in March.

In new elections, held in an atmosphere of terror, the Nazis still won only forty-four percent. But on the twenty-third of March, the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act, which allowed Hitler's government to make laws without parliament. Only the Social Democrats voted against it; the communist deputies had already been arrested or had fled. Within months, every other party was banned or dissolved itself. Trade unions were abolished. The states lost their independence. The process was called Gleichschaltung, the coordination of all German life under the Nazi Party.

Culture was purged. In May 1933, students burned books by Jewish, socialist and pacifist authors in Berlin and in university towns across the country. Artists, scientists and writers emigrated in their thousands, Albert Einstein and Thomas Mann among them. Joseph Goebbels, minister of propaganda, took control of the press, radio and film.

In June 1934, Hitler turned on his own movement. The SA, led by Ernst Röhm, had grown to millions of men and was demanding a second revolution, alarming the army. In the Night of the Long Knives, the SS murdered Röhm and dozens of other SA leaders, as well as conservative opponents. The army was grateful. When Hindenburg died in August, Hitler merged the offices of president and chancellor and became the Führer. Every soldier swore an oath of personal loyalty to him.

For many Germans, the following years felt like a recovery. Unemployment fell rapidly, thanks to public works like the motorways and, above all, to massive and secret rearmament. In 1935, Hitler announced conscription, openly breaking the Treaty of Versailles. In 1936, German troops reoccupied the demilitarised Rhineland, and Britain and France did nothing. That summer, Berlin hosted the Olympic Games, a carefully staged showcase of the new Germany.

Behind the façade, the police state grew. The Gestapo, the secret police, and the SS under Heinrich Himmler built a system of surveillance and terror that relied heavily on denunciations by ordinary citizens. And from the very beginning, the regime persecuted Germany's Jews, around half a million people, less than one percent of the population. In April 1933, there was a boycott of Jewish shops, and Jews were removed from the civil service. In 1935, the Nuremberg Laws stripped Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and other Germans. Step by step, Jews were pushed out of professions, schools and public life.

On the night of the ninth of November 1938, the regime unleashed a nationwide pogrom, later called Kristallnacht, the night of broken glass. Synagogues were burned, thousands of Jewish shops were destroyed, around a hundred people were killed, and some thirty thousand Jewish men were sent to concentration camps. Many Jews now tried desperately to leave, but most countries refused to take more than a few refugees.

Abroad, Hitler moved from success to success. In March 1938, German troops marched into Austria, which was annexed to the Reich amid cheering crowds. In September, at the Munich conference, Britain and France agreed to let Germany take the Sudetenland, the German-speaking border areas of Czechoslovakia, in the hope of preserving peace. Six months later, Hitler occupied the rest of the Czech lands. Britain and France finally guaranteed Poland's independence. In August 1939, Germany shocked the world by signing a non-aggression pact with its ideological enemy, the Soviet Union, with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe between them. Hitler now had a free hand. War was days away.

chapters.title: War and Genocide
chapters.text:
On the first of September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Two days later, Britain and France declared war. Poland was crushed within weeks, and the Soviet Union occupied its eastern half, as agreed in the secret pact. From the start, this was a war of a different kind. Behind the army came SS units that murdered Polish intellectuals, priests and Jews. The Nazis planned to turn Eastern Europe into living space for Germans, and its peoples into a population of slaves.

In the spring of 1940, Germany struck in the west. Denmark and Norway fell, then the Netherlands, Belgium and, in just six weeks, France. Hitler was at the height of his power. Only Britain, under Winston Churchill, kept fighting, and in the Battle of Britain the German air force failed to win control of the skies.

On the twenty-second of June 1941, Hitler launched his real war: the invasion of the Soviet Union, with more than three million soldiers. It was conceived from the start as a war of annihilation. Millions of Soviet prisoners of war were deliberately starved to death. Behind the front, mobile killing squads, the Einsatzgruppen, supported by police battalions and regular army units, shot Jewish men, women and children by the hundreds of thousands. At Babi Yar, near Kyiv, more than thirty-three thousand Jews were murdered in two days. The German advance reached the outskirts of Moscow but was stopped in December by the Soviet counterattack and the Russian winter. That same month, after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Hitler declared war on the United States.

The murder of the Jews of Europe now became systematic. In January 1942, at a villa on the Wannsee lake in Berlin, senior officials met to coordinate what they called the final solution of the Jewish question. Extermination camps were built in occupied Poland: Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, Chelmno, Majdanek, and the largest of all, Auschwitz-Birkenau. Jews were deported there by train from every corner of occupied Europe, from France and the Netherlands to Greece and Hungary, and murdered in gas chambers, most within hours of arrival. About six million Jews were killed in the Holocaust. The Nazis also murdered hundreds of thousands of Roma and Sinti, disabled people, and countless others they deemed enemies or inferior.

The turning point of the war came in the winter of 1942 to 1943, at Stalingrad, where an entire German army was surrounded and destroyed. In North Africa, German and Italian forces were defeated. From then on, the Red Army pushed relentlessly west. In June 1944, the Western Allies landed in Normandy. Germany's cities were being reduced to rubble by British and American bombers. Hamburg, Cologne, Dresden and Berlin were devastated, and hundreds of thousands of civilians were killed.

There was resistance in Germany, but it was small and isolated: communists and socialists, church figures, the students of the White Rose in Munich, and individuals who hid Jews. In July 1944, a group of army officers tried to kill Hitler with a bomb at his headquarters in East Prussia. Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg planted the bomb, but Hitler survived. Stauffenberg was shot that night in the courtyard of the army headquarters in Berlin, and thousands of suspects were arrested.

The last months of the war were the bloodiest. In January 1945, millions of Germans fled west before the advancing Red Army. In April, Soviet forces launched their final offensive across the Oder and encircled Berlin. Old men and teenage boys were sent to fight in the streets. In his bunker under the Reich Chancellery, Hitler killed himself on the thirtieth of April. Berlin surrendered on the second of May, and Germany capitulated unconditionally on the eighth of May 1945.

The war in Europe had killed more than thirty-five million people, among them some twenty-five million citizens of the Soviet Union. Germany lay in ruins. Germans would later call this moment Stunde Null, zero hour. Everything would have to begin again.

chapters.title: Division and Reunification
chapters.text:
In the summer of 1945, the victorious powers met at Potsdam, just outside Berlin. Germany lost its eastern territories to Poland and the Soviet Union, and around twelve million Germans were expelled or fled from Eastern Europe. What remained was divided into four zones of occupation: American, British, French and Soviet. Berlin, deep inside the Soviet zone, was divided into four sectors too. The women of Berlin, the Trümmerfrauen, began clearing the rubble by hand. At Nuremberg, the surviving Nazi leaders were put on trial.

The wartime alliance soon fell apart. The Soviets built a communist system in their zone, while the Western powers merged theirs and introduced a new currency, the Deutsche Mark. In June 1948, Stalin responded by blocking all land access to West Berlin. The Americans and British answered with the Berlin Airlift: for almost a year, planes landed every few minutes at Tempelhof and other airfields, supplying two million people with food and coal. Stalin gave up. The former enemy had become a partner.

In 1949, two German states were founded. In the west, the Federal Republic of Germany, with its capital in Bonn and Konrad Adenauer as chancellor, a parliamentary democracy anchored in the West and, from 1955, in NATO. In the east, the German Democratic Republic, the GDR, a one-party state under the Socialist Unity Party, closely controlled by Moscow. West Germany experienced an economic miracle, the Wirtschaftswunder. East Germany struggled. On the seventeenth of June 1953, workers rose up across the GDR, beginning on the Stalinallee in Berlin. Soviet tanks crushed the uprising.

The weak point was Berlin. Between East and West Berlin the border was still open, and East Germans could simply take the underground to the West. By 1961, around two and a half million people had fled, many of them young and skilled. On the night of the thirteenth of August 1961, East German soldiers and police sealed the border with barbed wire. Within days, they began building a wall. Families were separated overnight. Over the following years it grew into a deadly system of concrete walls, watchtowers, dogs and a death strip. At least a hundred and forty people were killed at the Berlin Wall trying to escape.

Berlin became the front line of the Cold War. In 1963, President Kennedy came to West Berlin and declared, Ich bin ein Berliner. In the GDR, the Stasi, the secret police, built one of the most extensive surveillance systems in history, with tens of thousands of officers and many more informers. In West Germany, a younger generation began to ask their parents what they had done under the Nazis, and the student movement of 1968 forced a reckoning with the past. In 1970, Chancellor Willy Brandt knelt at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto, and his Ostpolitik brought a cautious détente with the East.

In the 1980s, the Soviet Union, under Mikhail Gorbachev, began to reform. The GDR's ageing leader, Erich Honecker, refused to follow. In the summer of 1989, Hungary opened its border with Austria, and thousands of East Germans fled through it. In the autumn, mass protests spread across the GDR, above all in Leipzig, where every Monday tens of thousands marched with candles, chanting: We are the people. The protests stayed peaceful, and this time no tanks came. Honecker was forced out.

On the evening of the ninth of November 1989, a government spokesman, Günter Schabowski, announced at a press conference new rules allowing East Germans to travel. Asked when they would take effect, he looked at his notes and said: immediately, without delay. Thousands of East Berliners rushed to the border crossings. At Bornholmer Strasse, the overwhelmed guards finally opened the gate. That night, people danced on the Wall at the Brandenburg Gate. The ninth of November, the date of the republic in 1918 and of the pogrom in 1938, now became the date of freedom.

Eleven months later, on the third of October 1990, Germany was reunified. Berlin became its capital again, and the Reichstag, with its new glass dome, once more the home of a democratic parliament. As you walk through the city, you will see all these layers, often side by side: the Prussian monuments, the scars of war, the traces of the Wall, and the memorials with which Germany has chosen to remember, rather than forget, its past. Enjoy your journey.

series.title: Divided Berlin
series.subtitle: The Cold War, the Wall and the Stasi
series.intro: A deeper story in six chapters: how one city became the front line of the Cold War, how a wall was built through its heart, how a secret police watched an entire people, and how it all came down.

chapters.title: Ruins and Rivals
chapters.text:
Berlin, May 1945. The city that Hitler had wanted to rebuild as Germania, capital of the world, is a landscape of rubble. Around a third of its buildings are destroyed or damaged. There is no electricity, no running water, and very little food. Most of the men are dead, missing, or in prisoner-of-war camps, and it is the women of Berlin, the Trümmerfrauen, who start clearing the ruins, passing broken bricks from hand to hand in long human chains.

The Red Army had conquered the city alone, and for two months the Soviets were its only masters. Those weeks left deep scars. Soldiers looted, and many thousands of women were raped. At the same time, the Soviet military administration moved quickly to install its own people. On the thirtieth of April, a small group of German communists who had spent the war in Moscow, led by Walter Ulbricht, had landed east of Berlin. Ulbricht's instructions to his comrades were later remembered by one of them: it must look democratic, but we must have everything in our hands.

In July 1945, as agreed by the Allies, American, British and French troops arrived, and Berlin was divided into four sectors. The Soviets kept the eight eastern districts, including the historic centre around Unter den Linden. The Western sectors formed an island, more than a hundred and fifty kilometres inside the Soviet zone of occupation. In the British sector, almost next to the Brandenburg Gate, the Soviets built a memorial to their fallen soldiers, guarded by their own sentries. It would remain a Soviet outpost in the West for the next forty-five years.

The four powers were supposed to govern Germany together, but they soon disagreed about almost everything. In 1946, in the Soviet zone, the Social Democrats were forced to merge with the Communists into a new Socialist Unity Party, the SED. In West Berlin, Social Democrats voted against the merger in large numbers. In the city elections that October, the last free vote across all of Berlin until 1990, the SED came only third.

The decisive break came over money. On the twentieth of June 1948, the Western Allies introduced a new currency in their zones, the Deutsche Mark, and soon extended it to West Berlin. Stalin's answer was dramatic. On the twenty-fourth of June, Soviet forces cut every road, railway and canal into the Western sectors. Two million West Berliners had food for about a month and coal for even less. Stalin's calculation was simple: the Western powers would have to choose between abandoning Berlin and starting a war.

They found a third way. The American military governor, General Lucius Clay, and the British organised an airlift. At first it seemed impossible to feed a whole city by air, but the operation grew into a machine of extraordinary precision. At its peak, a plane landed in West Berlin every few minutes, at Tempelhof, at Gatow, and at Tegel, where Berliners built a new airfield in just three months. Planes carried flour, dried potatoes, medicine and above all coal. Over the next year, roughly two and a quarter million tonnes of supplies were flown in. Dozens of airmen died in crashes.

An American pilot named Gail Halvorsen started dropping sweets for the children watching at the end of the runway, tied to tiny handkerchief parachutes. Others copied him, and the airlift planes became known as the raisin bombers, the Rosinenbomber. Something important happened in those months. The Americans and the British, who had been bombing Berlin only three years earlier, became its protectors. In September 1948, three hundred thousand people gathered in front of the ruined Reichstag, and the mayor, Ernst Reuter, called on the peoples of the world to look upon this city.

In May 1949, Stalin lifted the blockade. It had failed completely. Days later, the Federal Republic of Germany was founded in the West, and in October, the German Democratic Republic in the East, with East Berlin as its capital. The airlift memorial in front of Tempelhof, with its three ribs pointing west, marks the beginning of the Cold War in Berlin. The city was not yet divided by a wall, but it was already split into two worlds.

chapters.title: The Workers' State
chapters.text:
The German Democratic Republic was founded on the seventh of October 1949, in the vast building on Wilhelmstrasse that had once been Hermann Göring's Air Ministry. Its leaders presented it as the better Germany: an anti-fascist state, built by workers and for workers, which had broken with the militarism and capitalism that had led to Hitler. Many sincere idealists believed in that promise, among them writers and artists who returned from exile to help build it.

The reality was a dictatorship modelled on Stalin's Soviet Union. Real power lay with the Politburo of the SED, and above all with its general secretary, Walter Ulbricht, a stiff, humourless functionary with a high-pitched Saxon voice. Industry was nationalised, large estates were broken up, and farmers were pushed into collectives. The Soviets dismantled entire factories and shipped them east as reparations. Opponents, real or imagined, disappeared into prisons, including former Nazi camps that the Soviet secret police reopened for new prisoners.

In 1950, the GDR created a Ministry for State Security, the Stasi, the sword and shield of the party. We will meet it again.

To show what socialism could achieve, Ulbricht launched a showcase project in the heavily bombed east of the city: the Stalinallee. Along a broad boulevard, workers built monumental apartment blocks in the Soviet style, faced with ceramic tiles, with high ceilings, central heating and lifts. These were palaces for the workers, and for those lucky enough to get a flat, they were a dream compared with the cold, crumbling tenements of the rest of the city.

But the economy was struggling, and in 1952 Ulbricht announced the accelerated construction of socialism. Prices rose, private businesses were squeezed, and in May 1953 the government raised work quotas by ten percent: workers would have to produce more for the same pay. On the sixteenth of June, construction workers on the Stalinallee put down their tools and marched to the House of Ministries on Wilhelmstrasse to protest.

The next day, the seventeenth of June 1953, the protest became an uprising. In Berlin and in hundreds of towns across the GDR, around a million people went on strike or took to the streets. The demands quickly moved beyond quotas: free elections, the release of political prisoners, the resignation of the government. Demonstrators tore the red flag from the top of the Brandenburg Gate.

The SED leadership took refuge with the Soviets, and the Soviets sent in the tanks. By evening, martial law had been declared and the uprising was crushed. At least fifty-five people were killed, and thousands were arrested. In the West, the street leading to the Brandenburg Gate was renamed the Street of the Seventeenth of June. In the East, the uprising was officially described as a fascist putsch organised by Western agents.

The playwright Bertolt Brecht, who lived in East Berlin, wrote a short poem in response, which was only published after his death. He asked, with bitter irony, whether it would not be simpler for the government to dissolve the people and elect another.

The lesson the regime drew was not to listen to its people, but to watch them more closely. The Stasi was expanded. And East Germans drew their own conclusion: if you could not change the system, you could still leave it. In Berlin, that was easy. The border between the sectors was open. You simply took the S-Bahn or the U-Bahn to the West, registered as a refugee at the reception camp in Marienfelde, and you were flown out to West Germany. Year after year, hundreds of thousands did exactly that.

chapters.title: Thirteenth of August
chapters.text:
By the end of the 1950s, the German Democratic Republic was bleeding to death. Since its founding, more than two and a half million people had left for the West, out of a population of around eighteen million. They were disproportionately young, and many were exactly the people the country could least afford to lose: doctors, engineers, teachers, skilled workers. Berlin, with its open sector border, was the hole in the Iron Curtain.

In November 1958, the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev issued an ultimatum: the Western powers must leave Berlin within six months, and it should become a demilitarised free city. The West refused, and the crisis dragged on for three years. Every rumour of new restrictions made more East Germans pack their bags. In July 1961 alone, thirty thousand people fled.

On the fifteenth of June 1961, at a press conference in East Berlin, a West German journalist asked Walter Ulbricht whether a state border would be built at the Brandenburg Gate. Ulbricht replied with a sentence that became infamous: nobody has the intention of building a wall. No one had mentioned a wall.

In fact, Ulbricht had been pressing Moscow for permission to close the border. In early August, Khrushchev agreed. The operation was organised in great secrecy by the party's security secretary, a man called Erich Honecker. Just after midnight on Sunday, the thirteenth of August 1961, police, soldiers and armed factory militias moved to the sector border. They tore up streets, strung barbed wire, and blocked the stations. When Berliners woke up that morning, their city had been cut in two.

The shock was immense. Families, couples and friends were suddenly separated. Some forty thousand East Berliners who worked in the West lost their jobs overnight. In the first days, the barrier was still improvised, and people took desperate chances. On the fifteenth of August, a nineteen-year-old border policeman named Conrad Schumann jumped over the barbed wire on Bernauer Strasse into the West, and a photographer captured the moment. The picture went around the world.

Bernauer Strasse was a special case. The houses on its southern side were in the East, but the pavement in front of them belonged to the West. Residents climbed out of their windows, or jumped, while West Berlin firemen held out nets below. On the twenty-second of August, a fifty-eight-year-old woman, Ida Siekmann, jumped from her third-floor flat and died of her injuries. She was the first known death at the Berlin Wall. The authorities soon bricked up the windows and evicted the residents.

Within days, the barbed wire was replaced by concrete blocks and hollow bricks: a wall. The Western powers protested, but did nothing more. The Wall did not touch their rights in West Berlin, and privately, President Kennedy remarked that a wall was a hell of a lot better than a war.

At the end of October, the tension almost exploded. East German guards began demanding identity papers from American officials crossing into East Berlin, which the Americans considered a violation of their rights. At Checkpoint Charlie, on Friedrichstrasse, General Clay ordered tanks to the border. On the twenty-seventh of October, Soviet tanks rolled up on the other side. For around sixteen hours, the two superpowers faced each other at a distance of a hundred metres, their guns loaded. Then, after a quiet exchange of messages between Washington and Moscow, the Soviet tanks pulled back a few metres, and the Americans followed. The division of Berlin had been accepted by both sides. The Wall would stand for twenty-eight years.

chapters.title: Living with the Wall
chapters.text:
The regime called it the Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart, and claimed it protected the GDR from Western aggression. Every guard knew the truth: it faced inwards. Over the years, the Wall became a sophisticated killing system around the whole of West Berlin, about a hundred and fifty-five kilometres long. Looking from the East, there was first an inner wall, then a strip of raked sand to show footprints, signal fences, anti-vehicle trenches, a patrol road, floodlights, watchtowers and dogs, and finally the outer wall, the one covered with graffiti on the Western side. Guards had orders to stop escapes by any means, including shooting.

On the seventeenth of August 1962, an eighteen-year-old bricklayer named Peter Fechter tried to climb the Wall near Checkpoint Charlie with a friend. The friend made it. Fechter was shot and fell back into the death strip, where he lay bleeding for almost an hour, calling for help, in full view of Western journalists and onlookers. Neither side intervened. He died there. At least a hundred and forty people were killed at the Berlin Wall, and many more along the inner German border.

And still people tried, with astonishing ingenuity. They hid in specially modified cars, crossed the river Spree, and flew over the Wall in home-made hot-air balloons. Above all, they dug. Students in West Berlin dug tunnels from cellars under the border. In October 1964, fifty-seven people crawled to freedom through a single tunnel under Bernauer Strasse, which became known as Tunnel 57.

For West Berliners, after the first years, the Wall became part of the landscape. Their city, an island of two million people, was kept alive with federal subsidies and a sense of defiance. In June 1963, President John F. Kennedy visited, and in front of the Schöneberg town hall, before a huge crowd, he declared, Ich bin ein Berliner. West Berlin became a magnet for young West Germans, partly because residents were exempt from military service, and it developed a famous alternative scene in districts like Kreuzberg, right up against the Wall.

For East Berliners, the West was visible from a few streets away and yet unreachable. Under the city, some West Berlin U-Bahn and S-Bahn lines passed through East Berlin. Their stations were closed and patrolled, and became ghost stations, where trains slowed down but never stopped. Friedrichstrasse station was the exception: a border crossing inside a railway station. Its departure hall, where East Berliners had to say goodbye to visiting relatives, became known as the Palace of Tears.

In the late 1960s, the West German chancellor Willy Brandt, who had been mayor of Berlin when the Wall was built, began a new policy towards the East, Ostpolitik: change through rapprochement. In 1971, the four powers signed an agreement guaranteeing access to West Berlin, and the two German states recognised each other the following year. Visits became easier, at least from West to East. That same year, Ulbricht was replaced by Erich Honecker, the man who had built the Wall.

The Cold War did not end, however. Berlin remained a capital of espionage. On the top of the Teufelsberg, a hill made of war rubble, the Americans and British listened to Soviet radio traffic. And on the Glienicke Bridge, between West Berlin and Potsdam, the two sides exchanged captured spies, starting with the American pilot Francis Gary Powers in 1962. The Wall, it seemed, was permanent. In January 1989, Honecker declared that it would still be standing in fifty, or even a hundred years.

chapters.title: The Stasi
chapters.text:
The Ministry for State Security, the Stasi, was founded in 1950. For thirty-two of its forty years, from 1957 until the end, it was run by one man: Erich Mielke, a communist who in his youth had shot two Berlin police officers in 1931 and fled to Moscow. Mielke ran his ministry from a huge complex in Lichtenberg, in eastern Berlin, which grew to more than forty buildings. His office, preserved exactly as he left it, is now part of the Stasi Museum.

The Stasi was a secret police, a foreign intelligence service, and a vast bureaucracy of surveillance, all in one. By 1989, it had around ninety-one thousand full-time employees, in a country of sixteen million people. Proportionally, that was far more than the Gestapo or the Soviet KGB. But its most powerful tool was its network of unofficial collaborators, the Inoffizielle Mitarbeiter, ordinary citizens who secretly reported on the people around them. In 1989, there were about a hundred and eighty-nine thousand of them. Over the history of the GDR, perhaps half a million people informed for the Stasi at some point.

They were colleagues, neighbours, pastors, doctors, friends, and sometimes husbands and wives. People became informers for many reasons: conviction, career, small privileges, or pressure and blackmail. The Stasi wanted to know everything. Officers opened letters, steamed open parcels and confiscated money sent from the West. They tapped telephones, hid microphones in apartments and cameras in watering cans, birdhouses and coat buttons. They even collected smell samples from suspects, cloths kept in sealed glass jars, so that dogs could track them later.

In the early years, the Stasi relied on open terror: arrests, show trials, and brutal interrogations. Its main remand prison in Berlin was in Hohenschönhausen, in a restricted area that did not appear on city maps. Prisoners were often driven there in vans disguised as delivery trucks, by detours, so that they had no idea where they were. In the 1950s, the cells in the basement, known as the U-Boat, were windowless and damp, and torture was common.

From the 1970s, as the GDR sought international recognition, the methods became quieter but no less cruel. The Stasi developed a technique it called Zersetzung, which means decomposition. Instead of arresting critics, it destroyed their lives from the inside. Officers spread rumours about them, sabotaged their careers, turned their friends against them, and broke into their homes to move furniture or change the pictures on the wall, so they would doubt their own sanity. Many victims never knew who was behind it.

The prisoners of the later years were people who had applied to leave the country, tried to escape, or written a forbidden poem. In Hohenschönhausen, they were rarely beaten. Instead, they were isolated, deprived of sleep, kept in uncertainty, and interrogated for months, until they signed confessions. Around a quarter of a million people were imprisoned for political reasons in the history of the GDR. Many were later bought free by West Germany, which paid hard currency for each prisoner released.

Why did the GDR need all this? Because the party never trusted its own people. The singer Wolf Biermann, whose songs mocked the regime, was banned from performing and, in 1976, stripped of his citizenship while on tour in the West. Writers, church groups, environmentalists and peace activists were infiltrated and watched. And yet the Stasi, with all its files, failed to understand what was coming. In the autumn of 1989, it reported precisely on the growing unrest, but it could not stop it.

chapters.title: We Are the People
chapters.text:
In 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev became leader of the Soviet Union. He spoke of glasnost, openness, and perestroika, restructuring, and he made it clear that Moscow would no longer send tanks to keep its allies in power. In Poland and Hungary, the communist parties began to negotiate with the opposition. In East Berlin, Erich Honecker refused to change anything. His regime even banned a Soviet magazine because it was too liberal.

The last person shot dead trying to cross the Berlin Wall was a twenty-year-old waiter, Chris Gueffroy, in February 1989. A few weeks later, in March, a man died when his home-made balloon crashed in West Berlin. Then, in May, Hungary began to dismantle the fence on its border with Austria. That summer, thousands of East Germans on holiday in Hungary did not come home. Others climbed into the gardens of the West German embassies in Prague and Warsaw. On the thirtieth of September, the West German foreign minister, Hans-Dietrich Genscher, appeared on the embassy balcony in Prague and announced that they would be allowed to leave for the West. The roar of the crowd drowned out the rest of his sentence.

Inside the GDR, people now found the courage to stay and protest. In Leipzig, prayers for peace in the Nikolai Church had been followed for weeks by small demonstrations. On the seventh of October, the regime celebrated its fortieth anniversary with a military parade in East Berlin, while Gorbachev, standing next to Honecker, was cheered by young people calling his name. Two days later, on Monday the ninth of October, seventy thousand people marched around the Leipzig ring road, carrying candles and chanting, We are the people. Hospitals had prepared extra blood supplies. But the security forces did not shoot. The fear had broken.

Honecker was forced out on the eighteenth of October. On the fourth of November, around half a million people filled Alexanderplatz in East Berlin, in the largest free demonstration in the history of the GDR. Then came the evening of the ninth of November. At a live press conference, the Politburo spokesman Günter Schabowski read out a note about new travel rules. A journalist asked when they would take effect. Schabowski shuffled his papers and said: as far as I know, immediately, without delay.

Within hours, thousands of East Berliners were at the border crossings. At Bornholmer Strasse, the officer in charge, Harald Jäger, received no orders and faced a growing crowd. At around half past eleven, he gave up and opened the gate. Other crossings followed. That night, strangers embraced, people climbed onto the Wall at the Brandenburg Gate, and West Berliners welcomed their neighbours with flowers and sparkling wine. In the following days, people chipped away at the Wall with hammers and chisels. They were called Mauerspechte, wall woodpeckers.

The Stasi, meanwhile, was busy shredding its files. When the shredders broke down, officers tore documents by hand. In December, citizens occupied Stasi offices across the country to stop the destruction. On the fifteenth of January 1990, demonstrators stormed the headquarters in Lichtenberg. Thanks to them, most of the files survived: more than a hundred kilometres of documents, plus thousands of sacks of torn paper that are still being pieced together today.

In March 1990, East Germans voted in their first and only free election. On the third of October 1990, the GDR joined the Federal Republic, and Germany was reunified. A year later, parliament passed a law that made a unique decision: the Stasi files would be opened to their victims. From January 1992, anyone could ask to read their own file. Millions have done so. Some discovered that their best friend, their brother, or their husband had reported on them for years.

Today, very little of the Wall remains. The longest stretch, along the river Spree, became the East Side Gallery, painted by artists from around the world. Elsewhere, a double row of cobblestones marks where it once stood. As you walk across that line in Berlin, you will barely notice it. That, perhaps, is the most remarkable thing of all.
